title: Nasdaq Futures Slip as Dismal Data‑Center IPO Hits Tech Investors – Live Market Updates Today
body:
Wall Street opened on a cautious note Tuesday, with Nasdaq‑100 futures slipping a fraction of a percent while a bruising debut by data‑center specialist Elice sent ripples through technology‑focused investors. The broader market showed mixed signals: the S&P 500 edged lower, the Dow Jones Industrial Average held near flat, and bond yields nudged higher as traders digested a blend of earnings reports, macro data, and renewed worries about the pace of artificial‑intelligence (AI) spending.

The most dramatic headline came from Hong Kong, where Elice – a privately held startup that builds modular, AI‑optimized data‑center infrastructure – listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong with a price that fell more than 30% from its opening level. The company’s valuation, which had been touted as a bellwether for the next wave of AI‑driven cloud capacity, quickly collapsed as investors questioned the sustainability of its business model amid a tightening funding environment. The sell‑off spilled over to other tech‑related equities across the Pacific, dragging Asian indices lower and prompting a modest pullback in U.S. tech stocks.

Analysts point to a confluence of factors that amplified the reaction. First, the AI hype that fueled a wave of capital inflows into data‑center builders earlier this year appears to be cooling. While demand for compute power remains robust, the sector’s capital‑intensive nature means firms must demonstrate clear pathways to profitability. Elice’s aggressive growth projections – promising to double capacity within 12 months – now seem optimistic in a climate where venture capital is becoming more selective. Second, the broader macro backdrop is less forgiving. Recent data showed U.S. consumer confidence slipping and inflationary pressures persisting, prompting the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates elevated. Higher rates increase the cost of borrowing for capital‑heavy projects, further dampening enthusiasm for speculative ventures.

The market’s reaction also reflects lingering anxiety over AI’s impact on corporate earnings. Earlier this week, several large technology companies released quarterly results that fell short of the lofty expectations set by AI‑driven revenue forecasts. Investors are now scrutinizing whether AI will translate into incremental profit growth or merely add to operating expenses. This skepticism was evident in the modest decline of Nasdaq futures, which fell about 0.2% in early trading, signaling that the rally that carried the index to record highs last month may be losing momentum.

Nevertheless, the downturn is not universal across the tech sector. Companies with established data‑center footprints, such as Equinix and Digital Realty, saw their shares hold steadier ground, buoyed by long‑term lease contracts and diversified customer bases. Moreover, a handful of AI‑focused chipmakers posted stronger‑than‑expected earnings, suggesting that while the infrastructure side may be under pressure, the demand for processing power remains a key growth driver. Investors appear to be re‑allocating capital from high‑risk, early‑stage players toward more mature firms that can weather short‑term volatility.

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching several indicators for clues on the trajectory of the tech rally. The upcoming earnings season will test whether AI can sustain higher margins, while the Federal Reserve’s policy meetings later this month could either reinforce the current rate stance or signal a shift toward easing, which would lower financing costs for data‑center expansion. In the meantime, the Elice episode serves as a cautionary tale that the AI boom, while transformative, still demands disciplined financial fundamentals. If the sector can balance aggressive growth with realistic profit expectations, the next wave of AI‑powered infrastructure could still deliver robust returns; otherwise, investors may see further pullbacks as the market recalibrates its appetite for risk.
